title: What should you ask first in a product launch case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a product launch case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Launch cases ask how to bring something new to market. Here is a simple way to cover everything that matters.
body:
The first question to ask

Is the decision to launch made, and what must the launch achieve?

How to build your structure

  • Who to target (segment size and growth, unmet needs, competitors in the segment)
  • What to offer (product, price, channels, message)
  • How to roll it out (capabilities, pilot then scale)
  • Does it pay? (expected sales, costs, break-even, cannibalisation)

The trap most people fall into

Choosing the 4Ps before choosing the customer.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the product launch framework.

Two prompts to try

How should an insurer launch weather insurance for small farmers in Kenya?

Show a model structure
  • Farmers' need: Losses from drought and floods; What they can afford
  • Product design: Payouts based on rainfall data; Price and cover
  • Distribution: Mobile money, co-operatives, seed sellers; Bundling with loans
  • Economics and risk: Claims in a bad year; Reinsurance, government support

Where to start: Distribution: reaching small farmers cheaply decides whether it works.

The trap: Designing a product farmers can't pay for or reach.

A launch plan should have a decision gate

A beverage company wants to introduce a sugar-free drink. Before recommending national advertising, ask whether the product solves a clear customer need and whether retailers will give it shelf space. Estimate the number of initial stores, expected units per store per week, the manufacturer’s net price and contribution per unit.

If 500 stores each sell 40 bottles weekly, the launch sells 20,000 bottles per week. At £0.35 contribution per bottle, that produces £7,000 weekly contribution before any launch overhead. A £200,000 launch campaign would take around 29 weeks to recover at that run-rate, and only if sales hold.

Pilot in a representative range of stores. Track trial, repeat purchase, gross margin, product returns, retailer reorder rate and impact on existing products. A successful product trial does not automatically justify national rollout if its sales mostly replace more-profitable products from the same manufacturer.
